run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_223 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Two tables exist in the configured SQL Server database: dbo.holmes_eval_223 and dbo.orders. The single row of dbo.holmes_eval_223 (id=1, category eval_test) carries verification_code HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9. For the slow-query question: dbo.orders has 10,000 rows, 1,000 distinct customer_id values (1..1000) and only one index, the clustered primary key on id; customer_id has auto-created statistics but no index key, so WHERE customer_id = 12345 has no seek path and must be evaluated against the clustered index. The predicate is highly selective (busiest customer_id has 21 rows), so an index on customer_id would be far cheaper. This is a strong hypothesis rather than a confirmed cause: no execution plan, logical-read or runtime measurement for this exact statement was obtained, and at 10,000 rows a scan is not intrinsically slow. Recommendations are advisory only; nothing was changed.

claims.text: The configured database contains exactly two tables, both in schema dbo: dbo.holmes_eval_223 and dbo.orders.
dbo.holmes_eval_223 has columns id (int, PK), category (nvarchar), verification_code (nvarchar) and created_at (datetime, default getdate()).
SELECT * FROM dbo.holmes_eval_223 returned one row: id=1, category=eval_test, verification_code=HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9, created_at=2026-11-21T08:49:50.483.
dbo.orders has five columns: id (int, PK), customer_id (int), order_date (date), total_amount (decimal), status (nvarchar).
The only index on dbo.orders is the clustered primary key PK__orders__3213E83FA0206300 on column id, with no included columns; no index has customer_id as a key column.
dbo.orders holds 10,000 rows, all in the clustered index PK__orders__3213E83FA0206300 (the only index listed by sys.partitions for this table).
dbo.orders has 1,000 distinct customer_id values, minimum 1 and maximum 1000, and currently 0 rows with customer_id = 12345 (the literal in the reported slow query lies outside the stored range).

Statistics exist on both id (PK__orders__3213E83FA0206300) and customer_id (auto-created _WA_Sys_00000002_38996AB5), so the optimizer has cardinality information on customer_id but no index key over it.
The predicate is highly selective: the largest per-customer order count observed is 21 rows (customer_id 707), followed by 20 (316), 19 (22), 19 (512), 18 (765) out of 10,000 rows.

The cached query-stats view filtered on text containing 'customer_id' returned two statements only — the INSERT INTO orders (...) load statement (10,000 executions, ~31,021 total logical reads) and the COUNT/DISTINCT aggregate used in this investigation — with no entry for the literal SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345.

The likely cause of the slowness is that dbo.orders has no nonclustered index whose key is customer_id: the only index is the clustered PK on id, so the customer_id equality cannot be served by a seek and must be evaluated by scanning the clustered index (10,000 rows today, growing linearly with table size), even though the predicate selects ~0.2% of rows.

SELECT * is a contributing factor: because all five columns (order_date, total_amount, status and the rest) are projected, even adding a narrow index on customer_id would require key lookups into the clustered index; a covering index or a narrower column list would be cheaper.

Other candidate causes remain unchecked and could also explain the perceived slowness: plan-cache/parameter-sniffing effects (plan cache holds no entry for this statement), blocking or lock waits on dbo.orders, and server-level resource pressure; none of these was measured.

At its current size, a clustered index scan of dbo.orders covers only 10,000 rows, so the observed data volume alone does not demonstrate that this query is slow; slowness at larger production scale is not shown by any measured runtime, logical-read or plan evidence in this Run.

Add a covering nonclustered index on the filter column, e.g. CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_orders_customer_id ON dbo.orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (order_date, total_amount, status); keep the id column as the clustering key so SELECT * can be satisfied from the index without key lookups, and weigh the extra write cost of the index on the INSERT load.

Confirm the diagnosis before and after any change by capturing the actual execution plan and logical reads for this exact statement (e.g. SET STATISTICS IO ON / actual execution plan in SSMS), which will show whether the plan is a clustered index scan and how many pages it reads; this Run did not obtain that plan.

gaps: No execution plan, logical-read count or elapsed time was obtained for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345: the query-stats lookup filtered on that literal text returned no rows, so the scan-versus-seek claim is inferred from the index definition, not measured.

The optimizer missing-index DMV query for dbo.orders returned no rows (status no_data), so no missing-index recommendation metadata was observed; DMV contents depend on plan cache state and restarts and an empty result is not proof of absence.
No latency baseline or historical trend for this query/table exists in this Run, and change_history is not integrated, so when the query became slow and whether the table grew cannot be established.

It is unknown whether customer_id 12345 is a valid business value: the stored range is 1..1000 and 0 rows match 12345, which may indicate an application-side id mismatch rather than, or in addition to, an indexing problem.
Blocking, lock waits, memory/CPU pressure and parameter-sniffing plans on dbo.orders were not checked and remain open candidate causes.
next_steps: Review the actual execution plan for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 in a controlled session and record logical reads before and after adding an index.
Create (after change approval) a covering nonclustered index on dbo.orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (order_date, total_amount, status) and re-measure.
Verify with the application owners whether customer_id 12345 is a legitimate id, given the stored range is 1..1000.
Check blocking/wait statistics and the cached plans for the workload that issues this query to rule out lock waits or a bad cached plan.
